1.pericope_label: Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish... The words of the wicked are to lie in wait for blood: but the mouth of the upright shall deliver them

schools.summary: Delitzsch weighs which half of the opening couplet is subject and which predicate before deciding for the fronted terms as predicates, finds in the word for wickedness the idea of wanting inward stay, renders the good wife as brave, and distinguishes the simple plans of the righteous from the tendentious schemes of the godless; Ellicott reverses the English of the first verse, fixes good as benevolent from the parallel, and glosses the wife as of power and character.

Gill widens instruction to the Scriptures, the ministry and the rod of affliction, insists that favour is drawn out by prayer rather than merited, and alone reads the settled state of the wicked eschatologically, of Babylon saying she sits a queen.

Clarke presses the Hebrew for reproof to mean discipline and the word for brutish to mean bear, grounds the permanence of goodness in its coming from God, and turns the virtuous woman into an essay on strength as the root of virtue; Wesley glosses the last verses in a line each.

Henry makes the opening couplet a test of whether one has grace, reads prosperity raised by sin as built on sand, makes the good wife's crown both ornament and ensign of power, and insists that thoughts are not free but under divine command.

debates.question: How is the opening couplet to be construed?

positions.view: The fronted terms are predicates: a man shows he loves knowledge by taking a learner's place.
The English order should be reversed: he that loves knowledge loves discipline.
The received order stands; correction is simply the road to knowledge.
It is a test of grace, since those who resent being told their faults are the brutish here meant.

debates.question: What makes the virtuous woman virtuous?

positions.view: Bravery or valour; she raises her husband to higher honour than the merely pleasant wife obtains.
Ability and character, as of the able men appointed judges.
Physical strength, taken literally, since where field labour falls to women it is the first qualification in a wife.
Piety and prudence in the management of the household.

outliers.note: Argues from African field labour and from the water-drawing of women in Judea that the strong wife of this verse is meant literally, and adds that a strong woman is likeliest to bear and rear healthy children.
Alone reads the settled prosperity of the wicked as prophecy of Babylon's fall, and the words that lie in wait for blood as the edicts of the beast.

themes: Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.
A good man obtaineth favour of the Lord: but a man of wicked devices will he condemn.
A man shall not be established by wickedness: but the root of the righteous shall not be moved.
A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones.
The thoughts of the righteous are right: but the counsels of the wicked are deceit.
The words of the wicked are to lie in wait for blood: but the mouth of the upright shall deliver them.

7.pericope_label: The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand... The wicked desireth the net of evil men: but the root of the righteous yieldeth fruit

schools.summary: Delitzsch weighs and rejects the reflexive reading of the opening verb, fixes the word for wisdom as intelligence throughout the book, defends the received text of the despised man with a servant, insists that the knowledge of a beast's state means its frame of feeling and not merely its provision, and takes the vain pursuits as things rather than persons; Ellicott offers judgments or storms for the overthrow and glosses the rest briefly.

Gill records without deciding the alternative that the man serves himself rather than keeps a servant, applies the overthrow to the fall of the beast and Babylon, and notes that the word for net may equally be rendered stronghold.

Clarke argues that the wicked seldom keep many generations in a direct line and finds a mercy in it, prefers the Latin version of the despised man outright, and turns the verse on the beast into an indictment of blood sports and wars of ambition; Wesley notes that the wicked man's cruelty mixes even into his mercies.

Henry adds the apples of Sodom to the overthrow, makes reputation follow piety and prudent conduct, calls it folly to covet a great figure abroad while wanting necessaries at home, and instances the proposal to chastise Christ and let him go as a pretended kindness.

debates.question: Are the wicked overturned, or do they turn about?

positions.view: Overturned; the parallel with the house of the righteous makes them the object, and the ancient versions agree.
The point is the suddenness, like the apples of Sodom that crumble at a touch.
The verse is about lineage: the wicked seldom keep many generations in a direct line.
Either God's judgments or the storms that overwhelm a house built on sand.

debates.question: Who is the despised man with a servant?

positions.view: A man of the middle rank, keeping the one slave that is an oriental's first necessity.
Either that, or a man who is servant to himself and does his own work.
The poor man who provides for himself, against the proud who would rather starve than do menial labour.
One who lives plainly at home rather than making a figure abroad.

outliers.note: Recounts finding the Hebrew of the clause about the beast painted on an inn sign, which reminded him to feed his horse, then turns the verse into an indictment of blood sports and wars of ambition.
Gathers the laws giving cattle the sabbath rest and their wages and requiring the dam to be let go, and calls them prefigurations of the righteous man's knowledge of his beast's feeling.

themes: The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand.
A man shall be commended according to his wisdom: but he that is of a perverse heart shall be despised.
He that is despised, and hath a servant, is better than he that honoureth himself, and lacketh bread.
A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread: but he that followeth vain persons is void of understanding.
The wicked desireth the net of evil men: but the root of the righteous yieldeth fruit.

13.pericope_label: The wicked is snared by the transgression of his lips: but the just shall come out of trouble... There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health

schools.summary: Delitzsch marks this as the turn to proverbs of the tongue, presses the consecutive form that makes the escape follow from the snare, distinguishes the fool's private opinion from objective criteria, quotes the saying that a man is known by his conduct in drink, money and excitement, and corrects the last verb to babbling; Ellicott adds the day of judgment to the snare, and independently reaches the same correction to babbling.
Gill offers a second construction under which the snare is laid for others rather than sprung on the speaker, and allows that a man may be satisfied by the fruit of another's mouth.

Clarke observes that a liar needs a good memory, matches the fool's wrath with the proverb that a fool's bolt is soon shot, and reports a manuscript variant making the verse speak of trusting in the piercings of a sword; Wesley defines the wise man as one who distrusts his own judgment.

Henry supplies the practical version at each turn, the lash for want of a bridle on the tongue, feeding on the bread we break to others, the fool who never enquires the way, and the tongue as death or life according to its use.

debates.question: What does it mean that the prudent man covers shame?

positions.view: He hides the dishonour done him so as not to increase his own injury; passionate self-defence is always evil.
Not ignoring the insult, but waiting for a convenient occasion to tell the offender of his fault.
He covers both the passion in his own breast, since anger is shame, and the provocation given him.
He conceals the injury and bears it with patience.

debates.question: What is the speech that pierces like a sword?

positions.view: Babbling: the verb means speaking at random, comparable to Greek words for stammering.
The text may instead read that a man trusts in the piercings of a sword, though the received reading is probably right.
Opprobrious words, slanders and whisperings that divide friends.

outliers.note: Reports a variant found in several manuscripts and an early polyglot that would turn the verse about piercing speech into one about trusting in a sword, while judging the received reading right.
Reads the snare of the lips forward to the day of judgment, words being the index of the soul and stored up as witness.

themes: The wicked is snared by the transgression of his lips: but the just shall come out of trouble.
A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth: and the recompence of a man’s hands shall be rendered unto him.
The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise.
A fool’s wrath is presently known: but a prudent man covereth shame.
He that speaketh truth sheweth forth righteousness: but a false witness deceit.
There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.

19.pericope_label: The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment... A prudent man concealeth knowledge: but the heart of fools proclaimeth foolishness

schools.summary: Delitzsch works through four attempts at the phrase for the lying tongue's moment before settling on the twinkling of an eye, defends the verse on devisers of evil against the charge of platitude, fixes the evil that befalls no righteous man as the harvest of sin, defines truth as probity between words and thoughts, and puts the concealing of knowledge under prudence; Ellicott makes the liar's detection providential and glosses the rest briefly.

Gill notes the root about ploughing evil and sowing discord, divides the evil that cannot befall the just into sin and punishment, and lists what lying contradicts in God, the Scriptures, the Gospel and the Spirit.

Clarke observes that falsehood gains credit only by being mistaken for truth, says God turns whatever occurs to the righteous man to his advantage, and supplies the blunt version that a silent fool may pass for wise; Wesley says liars are quickly convicted and that devisers of mischief bring trouble on themselves.

Henry contrasts the consistency of truth with the liar found in several stories, coins the epigram that deceivers will be deceived, offers a construction under which no evil happens to the just though the wicked be filled with spite, and adds the tag that the perfection of art is to conceal it.

debates.question: How long does a lying tongue last?

positions.view: The twinkling of an eye; the root is the swinging of a balance, and the cohortative marks a freely determined movement used to measure time.
Until examination finds the liar in several inconsistent stories.
Only so long as falsehood is mistaken for truth.
Until providence detects and silences it.

debates.question: In what sense does no evil befall the just?

positions.view: The evil meant is ethical wickedness, the harvest of sin, not misfortune in general.
Both the evil of sin, from which grace preserves, and the evil of punishment, which was laid on Christ.
Whatever occurs is turned to his advantage.
Possibly the whole verse means that no evil happens to the just though the wicked be filled with spite against them.

outliers.note: Defends the verse about devisers of evil against the charge of saying nothing, arguing that it asserts both the deception of the neighbour and the sorrow prepared for him.
Offers an alternative construction of the whole verse about evil and the just, reading the second half concessively rather than as a separate assertion.

themes: The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment.
Deceit is in the heart of them that imagine evil: but to the counsellors of peace is joy.
There shall no evil happen to the just: but the wicked shall be filled with mischief.
Lying lips are abomination to the Lord: but they that deal truly are his delight.
A prudent man concealeth knowledge: but the heart of fools proclaimeth foolishness.

24.pericope_label: The hand of the diligent shall bear rule: but the slothful shall be under tribute... In the way of righteousness is life; and in the pathway thereof there is no death

schools.summary: Delitzsch treats these verses as one group on the means of rising, reports the textual anomalies in the verse on heaviness of heart and keeps the received text, declares the verse on the righteous and his neighbour to yield no acceptable meaning as pointed and renders it of pastures, rejects the ancient rendering of the hunter's verb, and defends the negative against the preposition in the closing line; Ellicott supplies the forced labour of Solomon's works and takes the hunter's verb as netting.

Gill traces the diligent man's rise from apprentice to magistrate, argues that one righteous man cannot excel another since all are justified by the same righteousness, and offers the fowler's burning of captured wings as background to the hunter.

Clarke grounds the diligent man's rule in his independence, answers heaviness of heart with a single sentence of absolution, lists three ancient versions of the disputed verse and calls the Greek insufferable, prefers fraudulent to slothful in the hunter, and makes every duty a path to life; Wesley glosses the good word as compassionate.

Henry instances Solomon advancing Jeroboam, makes the deceitful rather than the merely lazy come under tribute, reads the righteous man's abundance as in the graces of the Spirit, and takes the way of righteousness as a highway cast up by God with life in it and not only at its end.

debates.question: What does the verse about the righteous and his neighbour mean?

positions.view: No acceptable meaning comes from the traditional pointing; it should read that the righteous looks after his pastures.
The pasture rendering cannot be got from the Hebrew; the received sense is best, the poor righteous man excelling his affluent neighbour.
Either the comparative sense, or that the just man guides his neighbour while the wicked wanders.
The comparison holds strictly only against an unrighteous neighbour, since all the righteous share one righteousness.
The righteous is more abundant, in the graces and comforts of the Spirit.

debates.question: What does the slothful man fail to do with his prey?

positions.view: Roast or singe it; the ancient rendering of catching has no warrant in the stem.
Net or secure it.
The word is fraudulent rather than slothful, and justice snatches the gain from his mouth.
He roasts what others hunted, living on the fruit of their labours like a drone.

outliers.note: Rests the closing promise of immortality on a single vowel, arguing that all the old versions misread the negative as a preposition and that the Babylonian pointing distinguishes the two.
Sets three ancient versions of the disputed verse side by side and rejects the Greek as insufferable for making the righteous man his own friend.

themes: The hand of the diligent shall bear rule: but the slothful shall be under tribute.
Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad.
The righteous is more excellent than his neighbour: but the way of the wicked seduceth them.
The slothful man roasteth not that which he took in hunting: but the substance of a diligent man is precious.
In the way of righteousness is life; and in the pathway thereof there is no death.
